Welcome. I’m so glad you’re here, ready to step into a story where longing, loss, and the search for meaning come alive through every page.
Imagine a life shaped by the beauty—and sometimes the ache—of our connections with others. Together, we’ll wander through memories shaped by family, faith, and the quiet wonders of the natural world. There’s something powerful about how our hearts hold both desire and disappointment, and how those moments can reveal who we truly are.
In Every Natural Heart: A Memoir, James Dobson invites us to walk beside him as he explores the landscape of his past. This isn’t just about revisiting memories—it’s about meeting vulnerability and resilience head-on, and discovering the quiet moments that end up defining us. Through his honest reflections, we’ll see how love, grief, and hope are all woven into the tapestry of everyday life.
As the seasons shift, so does the story—moving through the bonds between parent and child, the ties to community, and the ongoing dance between the sacred and the ordinary. We’ll trace the path of those formative experiences, the little revelations, and the big questions that shape who we are.
So, if you’re ready for a journey that’s both intimate and universal, let’s explore these pages together. We’ll uncover what it really means to be alive—to hold both the pain and the wonder in our hands, and to find meaning in every natural heart.

Chapter 1: Childhood in a New Land—The Weight of Family and Memory
Picture a small American town. The streets are familiar—there are shops, schools, neighbors who offer a quick nod as they pass by. But step inside one particular home, and everything changes. The air is thick with the sound of Armenian words, the scent of old recipes, and the quiet ache of parents who’ve left their whole world behind.
For this child, growing up here means living in two worlds at once. The rhythms of Armenian speech fill the house, and the stories—sometimes whispered, sometimes blurted out in anger or sadness—cling to the walls. You can almost feel the weight of memories, carried like invisible luggage by parents who have survived so much. Their hope for a better life hangs heavy in every room.
But outside? School is a different universe. There, the child is just another face in the crowd, expected to blend in, speak perfect English, and laugh at jokes that don’t quite make sense at home. Even lunchtime feels like a test—imagine opening a lunchbox full of foods that no one else recognizes, feeling embarrassed while classmates trade sandwiches. And every time the teacher stumbles over their name, it’s another reminder of just how different they are. Most kids don’t notice. But for this child, there’s always a delicate balancing act: honoring family at home, while desperately wanting to fit in at school.
Back at home, the parents work long, exhausting hours—jobs that barely pay, and never offer the respect they once knew. The father, who was once so proud back in Armenia, now faces the grind of factory work. The mother’s hands are always busy, her eyes always alert, keeping the family afloat with sheer determination. Their sacrifices are both a comfort and a burden. The child feels an unspoken pressure to do well, to make all that suffering worthwhile, while also knowing—deep down—it’s impossible to ever repay what’s been given.
Family gatherings are a bittersweet mix. Relatives come together, sharing stories of the old country—sometimes laughing until they cry, other times just crying. The food, the music, the little rituals—they’re all ways to keep the past alive, to remind everyone who they are. But beneath all the celebration, there’s a quiet fear: what if these traditions fade away? What if the next generation forgets?
As the child grows, new questions bubble up. What does it really mean to belong? Can you be both Armenian and American, or do you always have to choose? The answers keep shifting—sometimes there’s pride in heritage, a hunger to share it; other times, the urge to just disappear into the crowd is almost too strong to ignore.
In the end, memory becomes the anchor. Stories at the dinner table, photos on the mantel, songs sung late into the night—all these things hold the family together, even as the world around them changes. But memory also stings. It’s a reminder of what’s been lost, and what can never quite be recovered.
So, in these early years, the child starts to realize something important: identity isn’t set in stone. It’s shaped by family, by culture, and by that constant tug-of-war—the need to belong, and the need to remember where you came from. The journey’s just beginning, and already, it’s marked by both hope and uncertainty.

Chapter Two: The Struggle to Belong—Navigating Two Worlds.
As you reach those teenage years, something changes. Suddenly, the world inside your home and the world outside feel like two different planets. At home, the rules are set in stone—show respect, honor your traditions, work hard, and never lose sight of your roots.
But once you step outside, it’s a whole new game. Fitting in means being independent, blending in, and chasing dreams that sometimes look nothing like the ones your family had in mind.
School quickly becomes more than just a place to learn—it’s where you fight to figure out who you are. You do well in class, maybe because you want to make your family proud, or maybe to prove that being different doesn’t mean you’re any less. Still, there’s this constant feeling of being on the outside looking in. Friends share stories about family vacations, American holidays, moments from childhood that you can’t quite relate to. Sure, you laugh along, but deep down, you wish someone really understood.
Then there are sports and social events—opportunities to connect, but also moments where the differences stand out. You’re invited to a party, and suddenly you’re worried. What should you wear? What do you say? How do you act so you don’t draw the wrong kind of attention? Sometimes, it just feels safer to stay home, to avoid the risk of standing out or making a mistake.
Meanwhile, your parents see you changing. They notice you pulling away, and it scares them. Maybe they argue with you about little things—your clothes, your friends, your taste in music. But underneath it all, there’s a deeper fear: that you’ll forget everything they’ve worked so hard to keep alive, that you’ll drift so far you become a stranger.
Stuck in the middle, you feel torn. There’s guilt for wanting something different, for dreaming of a future that doesn’t revolve around family traditions. At the same time, you can’t help but feel frustrated—like your parents just don’t get what it’s like to grow up somewhere completely new.
And yet, every once in a while, there’s a spark—maybe it’s sharing a meal, swapping stories late at night, or hearing a song that takes everyone back to the old days. In those moments, you realize just how much love and strength has carried your family this far.
You start to see that this struggle to belong isn’t just about you—it’s part of something bigger. It’s about survival, adaptation, and hope.
Little by little, you learn that you don’t have to choose one world over the other. Maybe, just maybe, you can find a way to hold onto both. It’s a process—a journey of honoring where you come from, while still reaching for what’s ahead. And while the road isn’t easy, there’s a growing sense that it is possible—to build a life that feels both rooted and free.

Chapter 3. The Power of Art: Finding a Voice Through Creativity
Imagine you’re caught in a swirl of confusion and longing—everything feels a bit off, and you’re searching for something that makes sense.
Then, out of nowhere, a new possibility opens up. Art—whether it’s writing, drawing, or music—suddenly becomes a way to piece the world together. For a teenager, creativity offers this secret space, almost like a hidden room where the usual rules just don’t apply. It’s a place to explore feelings and ideas that never seem to fit into everyday life.
And it all starts quietly. Maybe it’s a poem scrawled in the corner of a notebook, a quick sketch during a dull class, or even a melody softly hummed when no one’s listening. At first, these little acts of creation are just for you—a way to work through emotions that feel way too tangled to talk about. But, over time, they start to grow into something bigger. They become a bridge, a way to connect with others—to say what you can’t just blurt out in a conversation.
So, art turns into a lifeline. It helps you survive the pressure from family, and the challenge of fitting into a new world. Through stories and images, you find your voice. Suddenly, you have a way to speak your truth. Creating becomes both a safe haven and a quiet rebellion—a way to carve out space in a world that can feel pretty unwelcoming.
Of course, parents don’t always get it. They worry art is a distraction, maybe even a luxury that you can’t really afford. They want you to focus on what’s practical, to choose a path that feels secure and brings respect. That leaves you pulled in two directions—wanting to honor your parents, but still feeling that unstoppable pull toward creativity.
Then, someone steps in—a teacher, a mentor—someone who spots your spark and actually encourages it. This adult gives you guidance, support, and, maybe most important of all, real belief in what you can do. For the first time, you feel truly seen. Not just as an immigrant kid, not just as someone’s child—you’re recognized as an individual who has something unique to offer.
Through art, you start to work out all those contradictions in your life. The stories from the old country, the struggle to fit in, the longing to belong—they all find a place in your poems, your paintings, your songs. Creating becomes a way to honor where you’ve come from, while also forging your own path forward.
And before long, it’s clear—art isn’t just a hobby. It’s a necessity. It’s how you survive, how you heal, how you rise above your circumstances. Every act of creation is really an act of hope—a statement that life can be meaningful, even when things feel uncertain or you’re facing loss.

Chapter Four: Family Ties and the Burden of History
As you step into adulthood, you might notice just how strong the pull of family can be. Suddenly, your parents—now older, maybe a bit more fragile—turn to you for comfort and support. Their expectations can feel heavy at times, can't they? But then, so does the love that holds you all together.
Family gatherings start to mean something different. The old stories, once confusing or even a little boring, now feel precious. You find yourself listening more closely to tales of the "old country," realizing just how much courage and resilience it took for your family to get where they are. There’s this new sense of gratitude, a growing urge to honor the sacrifices that shaped your journey.
But let’s be honest—the weight of history is real. The trauma from the past—wars, displacement, loss—it all lingers in the background. Sometimes, you feel this invisible pressure to make it all worthwhile, to turn your family’s suffering into something meaningful. And maybe, there’s a little guilt for wanting something different—for dreaming of a life that doesn’t revolve around duty or tradition.
That tug-of-war between your own desires and family obligations can get intense. Every decision, big or small—your career, your relationships, even your daily choices—seems to come with a side of family expectations. There’s a longing for freedom, but also a real fear of letting down the people who’ve given you so much.
When you pause to reflect, it’s clear: the past isn’t something you can just walk away from. The stories, the memories, the family rituals—they’re woven into who you are now. The real challenge? Figuring out how to carry that history without letting it weigh you down.
Sure, there are arguments. Misunderstandings that feel impossible to fix. But there are also those moments that remind you why it all matters—a shared laugh, a simple act of kindness, or that quiet, wordless understanding. Through everything, the bonds of family hold strong, shaped by both love and loss.
Gradually, you start to see that resilience isn’t just about surviving tough times. It’s about finding meaning in them. Your family’s story is one of endurance, adaptation, and hope. And when you really embrace that legacy, you discover a path forward—one that lets you honor where you’ve come from, while still making space for your own future.

Chapter 5: Embracing Identity — Honoring Heritage While Forging a New Path
Over time, that struggle to fit in starts to change. Instead of feeling pulled between two worlds, you begin to see yourself as a blend of many experiences—like a tapestry made up of all the threads from your past, your present, and your hopes for the future.
The road hasn’t been easy. There’ve been plenty of moments where you felt lost, or doubted where you belonged. But then, slowly, those moments of clarity show up—when you realize the puzzle pieces are finally coming together.
You start to notice how your childhood stories, the challenges you face right now, and the dreams you’re chasing all belong to the same bigger picture. They’re not competing—they’re connected.
Creativity keeps playing a huge role. Through art—whether it’s painting, writing, or music—you get to explore what it really means to belong, to be part of a family, to understand yourself. Every time you create, it’s not just about keeping your heritage alive; it’s also a way to show the world who you are, on your own terms. Art isn’t just for getting by—it’s for growing, and thriving.
And as time passes, your relationships with family change, too. Maybe once your parents felt like a source of pressure or conflict. But now, they become partners—fellow travelers on this journey. There’s a new kind of understanding. You realize that every generation has to find its path, and you learn to forgive, to let go of old grudges, and to notice the love that’s always been there, sometimes quietly.
Even the process of fitting in—what used to feel so painful—starts to look different. You see that moving between cultures, adapting, and learning to survive has actually given you a kind of strength. You can now take pride in both your roots and your individuality, embracing every side of your identity.
Looking back, you realize this journey was never just about getting by. It’s about finding meaning in your memories, about finally feeling like you belong, and about learning to love not only where you came from, but where you are now. And in this way, your story becomes something everyone can relate to—a reminder that we all carry history with us, but we also have the power to create something new.
The journey’s not over, but there’s a new sense of peace. You find yourself standing right at the crossroads of past and future—rooted in your heritage, but open and ready for whatever comes next.
And maybe, for the first time, your heart feels whole.

Chapter 6: The Call of the Old Country—Returning to the Source
Have you ever felt that tug—the one that starts deep inside you, pulling you back toward your roots? There comes a point when the stories you’ve heard and the memories you’ve carried just aren’t enough anymore. Suddenly, the urge to see the land your ancestors called home is so strong, you can’t ignore it.
So, the decision’s made. It’s not easy—there’s excitement, sure, but also this quiet fear. What if you don’t fit in? What if you’re seen as a stranger in the very place that shaped your family’s history?
Picture yourself stepping onto a plane, carrying more than just your suitcase. You’re carrying generations of hopes, dreams, and unanswered questions. When you finally land in Armenia, the view out the window feels both familiar and completely new. The language you used to hear at home suddenly surrounds you. Faces in the crowd echo the features of people you’ve only seen in faded photos. The rhythm of life here? It sounds a lot like the stories your parents and grandparents used to tell.
Meeting distant relatives is a mix of comfort and awkwardness. There are hugs that linger, tears that surprise you, and laughter that fills the room. And yet, there are also those moments when words just aren’t enough—when you realize that, while you share blood, years apart have shaped you differently. But even then, there’s this undeniable sense of coming home. You feel like some part of you has been waiting for this all along.
As you wander through old streets, step into churches, and browse bustling markets, you can’t help but notice the resilience in the people around you. The scars of history are visible—monuments that speak of loss, memories that refuse to fade. And yet, life carries on. Kids play in the alleys, elders gather to swap stories, and the everyday rhythm never misses a beat. It hits you that the past isn’t just something heavy to carry—it’s also a source of strength.
Then, there’s that afternoon when you finally see the village where your parents were born. The old house is gone, replaced by something new, but the land—the land is the same. Standing there, you feel a connection that words can’t really express. It’s a sense of belonging that’s both incredibly deep and somehow just out of reach. For a moment, everything feels clear. You realize your identity isn’t just rooted in memories—it’s tied to this place, too.
Heading back, you know this isn’t the end of your story. It’s a fresh beginning. You leave with a heart that’s a little quieter, but a whole lot fuller. The pain and beauty of your heritage are woven together now, and the stories you’ve carried have taken on new meaning. You’re ready to carry them forward—to let them shape the next chapter of your journey.

Chapter 7: Love, Loss, and the Search for Home
Life in America keeps moving forward. Maybe you’re building a career, making new friends, or even starting a family of your own. But even as everything changes on the outside, those old questions about where you belong and who you really are—they don’t just vanish, do they?
And then, love comes into the picture. It sweeps in with all its joy and complexity. There’s that excitement—maybe even a little fear—when you fall for someone. You start imagining a life together, hoping to build something brand new. But it’s not always simple. Sometimes, your past shapes how you love. You’re trying to honor what came before, while also wanting to create something that’s truly yours.
Falling in love is thrilling, but let’s be honest—it can be a little scary too. There’s the spark, the feeling that you’ve found your person. But challenges come up. Maybe you and your partner have different backgrounds, different dreams, or different ways of seeing the world. Suddenly, you’re facing those same tensions you once had with your parents—the tug between tradition and independence.
And sometimes, love doesn’t last. Heartbreak hurts, sometimes more than you expect. But even in that pain, there’s room for growth. In those quiet moments afterward, you start to wonder: what does it really mean to build a home? You realize it isn’t just about a physical place. It’s about creating a sense of belonging, day by day, with the people and choices you make.
Friendships become even more important now. There’s a special comfort in being with people who truly get what you’re going through—folks who’ve walked a similar path. Sharing a meal, talking late into the night, laughing until you can’t breathe—these moments build a kind of chosen family. You find that belonging isn’t about fitting in; it’s about being seen and accepted for who you really are.
Of course, loss touches everyone. Losing loved ones—whether it’s parents, relatives, or close friends—brings a wave of grief. But it also makes you cherish the bonds that remain. You learn to carry both sorrow and gratitude, honoring those who are gone while still reaching for hope and love in your own life.
Over time, the search for home shifts. It’s less about where you are on the map and more about the connections you build. Home starts to look like shared moments of kindness, or the act of making meaning from your memories. The journey isn’t over yet—but with each step, you find a little more peace, knowing that home is something you create, together with the people you love.

Chapter 8. The Next Generation: Passing Down Stories.
Time keeps moving, doesn’t it? And with every year, there’s this growing feeling—almost a gentle responsibility—to pass along the family’s story to those coming up behind us.
Maybe you’re a parent, an aunt or uncle, or just the natural storyteller in your circle. Either way, you can feel the weight of that legacy, especially when you look at the kids in your life. They’re so full of questions—curious about where they come from, and quietly searching for who they are.
Sharing these stories brings all kinds of emotions. There’s real joy in it, but let’s be honest—it isn’t always easy. You want to protect kids from the toughest parts of the past. At the same time, you know deep down that understanding history is essential for them.
So, you find those moments—maybe it’s around the dinner table, at bedtime, or during a long, meandering walk—and you begin to tell the stories. Tales of courage, loss, and survival. Sometimes, the kids listen with eyes wide open, hanging on every word. Other times, they’re a little impatient, fidgeting, but that spark of curiosity is always there.
Of course, there are moments when you wonder—will these stories really matter? Will the next generation care enough to carry them forward? The world changes so fast, and the pull to fit in, to blend with everyone else, is strong.
But then, you notice little things—a child asking for that special family dish, quietly humming a song from the old country, or tossing out a phrase that’s been in your family for generations. That’s when you know: the stories are taking root.
Storytelling turns into a bridge, connecting the past with the present. You start to let go of the idea that every detail has to be perfect. What really matters is the heart of it all—the spirit of resilience, and the hope woven through every chapter.
And here’s the beautiful part: as you share these stories, something shifts in you, too. There’s a sense of healing. Honoring the journey of those who came before helps you make sense of your own path, and it gives the next generation a true sense of belonging.
In the end, these stories become a gift. It’s your way of saying, “You’re not alone. You’re part of something bigger.” And that simple truth? It makes all the difference.

Chapter 9: Art as Legacy—Creating Meaning from Memory.
As time moves on, creativity doesn’t just fade into the background—it becomes an old friend, right by your side. Maybe you’re a little older now, a bit wiser, and you’ve found yourself turning to art, not just to get through tough times, but to make sense of your life, to express who you are. And, more and more, you realize that what you create isn’t just for you—it’s something you’ll leave behind, a piece of yourself for the people who come after.
Art shows up in so many ways. Maybe it’s writing, painting, music—or even the love you put into a homemade meal, or the care you give to a garden. Every act of creation is like a thread, weaving together your family’s story, your culture, your memories. And there’s real joy in sharing what you’ve made, in watching other people connect with the stories and images that shaped your own journey.
Of course, there are days when doubt creeps in. Maybe you wonder if your art matters, or if anyone’s really paying attention. Life gets busy, and sometimes it’s hard to find the space to be creative. But here’s something important—art isn’t really about fame or applause. It’s about being honest, about honoring all the messy, beautiful parts of life. It gives a voice to things you might never say out loud.
Sometimes, you find yourself guiding others. Maybe you’re mentoring a young person who’s still searching for their own way to express themselves, or you’re helping an elder share the stories they’ve carried for years. These moments—teaching, collaborating—remind you that creativity isn’t a solo act. It’s something we share, something that brings people together.
And when you look back, you see it clearly—art has been your lifeline. It helped you survive, it helped you heal, and it connected you to others in ways nothing else could. There’s so much gratitude for the gift of creativity, and for every chance you’ve had to share it.
In the end, the legacy of art isn’t just what you create—it’s all the lives you touch along the way.

Chapter 10: Coming Full Circle—Acceptance and Renewal.
As life moves forward, it really does feel like the journey comes full circle, doesn’t it? Maybe now, you’re looking back—not just as an adult, but perhaps as a grandparent, or an elder. Think about that path: the struggles you faced as a child, the rollercoaster of adolescence, all the ups and downs of adulthood. In the end, they’re all part of a much bigger story.
What you start to notice is a gentle sense of acceptance settling in. You realize that identity? It’s never been fixed—it’s always changing and growing. Over time, you’ve learned how to hold onto both joy and sorrow, to honor where you’ve come from while opening your arms wide to the present. The heart, once pulled in different directions, feels whole at last.
Family, of course, remains right at the center of everything. But these relationships—they’ve changed too. There’s more patience now, a deeper understanding, and a real appreciation for how love can stretch and endure through every season. Joy isn’t always in the big milestones anymore. Sometimes, it’s found in the simplest things: sharing a meal, having a quiet conversation, or hearing a child’s laughter fill the room.
Sure, the world keeps turning, always shifting. The challenges of fitting in, of figuring out who you are, they’re still there. But now, there’s no fear. Instead, there’s a kind of peace—a quiet trust that the next generation will find their own way, just like you did. The stories you’ve lived, the art you’ve created, the memories you hold—they become gifts. Things you pass on, hoping they’ll help light the way for those who come after.

As we wrap up our time with "Every Natural Heart," I hope you’re feeling a little more seen on your own path. You know, the journey of identity—it's hardly ever a straight shot. It twists and turns, shaped by our memories, our families, and the choices we make every single day. This isn’t just a story about one family or one heritage. It’s about all of us—anyone searching for a place to belong, finding the courage to honor where we come from, and daring to build something new from what we've inherited. So, here are a few gentle truths to take with you:
Identity isn’t set in stone. It grows and changes as we do, shaped by the memories we hold and the choices we make. Even the hardest family stories can be a source of strength, if we let them bring us closer together. Creativity isn’t just a nice-to-have—it’s how we process, honor, and make sense of our experiences. Real belonging? It lives in the people we love, not just in old traditions or familiar places. And, every time you share a story, you’re giving a gift to the future—passing on love in a way that lasts. You don’t need to figure everything out right now. It’s enough to keep asking questions, to really listen to the stories that surround you, and to trust that your own journey is important. Sure, the past can feel heavy. But it’s also full of hidden treasures—resilience, hard-earned wisdom, and the seeds of fresh beginnings. So as you move forward, let yourself be rooted in where you’ve come from, but stay open to change and new growth. Carry your history with pride, and leave space for what’s next. After all, the heart is made to long for connection—and it’s built to heal, to create, and to love. Here’s to your journey, wherever it leads.
